title.en: Ussungussak or Savnimersok: The Inlander's Seal-Trap
title.zh: 烏蘇恩瓜舒克：內陸人的捕豹陷阱

region.en: Gulf of the earth and the inland meadow

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; two of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Scolded empty-handed once too often, Ussungussak follows a beach-stranger inland through the fearful precipice of the earth's gulf — nearly choked by a cord round his neck — to an inlander's comfortable house, whose shore-standing trap kills seals on the beach. Given leave to take one at a time, then two, greed carries him past the last of the lot; refused a return when he comes empty again, he is fairly strangled at the precipice — and the kayaker sent to find him avenges him with harpoon, bladder, and arrow, putting a knee on the nape of the giant he has cut up.
summary.zh: 又一次空手而歸、被妻子痛罵的烏蘇恩瓜舒克，跟隨岸邊的陌生人走進內陸——穿越大地之灣的可怕絕壁，頸上繩索勒得他幾乎斃命——抵達內陸人舒適的家。那內陸人立於岸上以陷阱獵豹，沙灘上堆滿死豹。許他一次取一、再取兩頭；貪心令他把最後一頭也搬空。空手再來時，他在絕壁處被活活勒死；出海尋找他的皮艇客以魚叉、浮囊、箭連環報仇，踩著已肢解的巨人後頸。

sensitivity.note: Rink gives the tale for its apparent mythological reference, noting it is otherwise fragmentary and obscure. The earth's gulf precipice is an otherworld threshold motif.

passages.text: A number of people once lived together in a large house; among them was a man named Ussungussak, who generally came home empty-handed when all the others returned with what they had caught, for which his wife used to scold him. One night she had gone on rating him worse than usual, and in the morning he had disappeared. He kayaked along shore, and having rounded a point saw a man standing on the beach; at first he was frightened, but then he thought a little and finally concluded, 'Why should I be afraid at the very moment I have resolved to go and lead a solitary life all by myself?' When the man on shore called him, he alternately approached and again turned back; but when he had come pretty close to the beach, the other threw out a trap, by which he drew him in, and ordered him to follow to the inland. They wandered along together and came to the gulf of the earth; there poor Ussungussak began to whine and howl, but the inlander put a cord round his neck, straining it so hard that he was nearly choked — when he again untied him, however, they had safely passed the fearful precipice. Having next crossed a beautiful meadow, they gained the house of the inlander, who had a wife but no children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning Ussungussak was ordered to remain at home, while the master of the house went away himself and returned very noisily in the evening with what he had taken; in this way several days went by, but at length Ussungussak got desirous to see his own home, and the inlander accompanied him on the way. This time they did not see the precipice; arriving at the coast they saw a great many killed seals on the beach, being those which the inlander, standing on shore, had caught in his trap. When Ussungussak was about to take leave, the inlander said, 'Henceforth thou canst take some of these seals, but mind, thou art not to be too greedy: thou mayst take one at a time to begin with; afterwards thou mayst take two.' He returned to his homestead and housemates, who were having good hunting at the time; the next day he again disappeared, but in the evening returned with two seals; the following day he brought home three — 'Out at the most seaward place,' he answered, when asked where he had got them, and they demanded whether they might not accompany him thither.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But when he had carried away the very last of the lot, he one night returned without anything at all, and was again scolded by his wife. The day after he left as before, kayaking along shore he at length turned a point and again beheld the inlander; this time he willingly approached him when he was called and went along with him — but when they had gained the precipice, he did not get over this time, but was fairly strangled. When Ussungussak's relations and housemates had been expecting him in vain for five days, one of the kayakers went out in search of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He encountered the inlander, and asked him whether he had not seen a man — 'To be sure I have, and I killed him myself!' At this the other thrust his harpoon at him, and he ran on with the hunting-bladder dragging behind him, and thus disappeared; the coastman now took his spear and bladder-arrow, following him swiftly, and found him drawing out the point — he lanced another spear at him, while the inlander kept running on so fast that the bladder flew up high in the air; finally he flung his arrow at him, and this at last did for him, and he expired, upon which the pursuer cut him up, and put his knee on the nape of his neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Child-Monster with Great Big Teeth

region.en: Great rock and provision-house, inland country
region.zh: 巨巖與糧倉之間的內陸

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Born with great big teeth that tear the midwife's arm, the monster drags its own mother by the loose hair and devours the whole settlement — eating away the boat-pillars, ordering the refuge-rock itself to upset. Two boys and their sister escape to the provision-house, flee houses where the sleepers plot to kill them, spell one house-door dead with the brother's boot, and are saved by a giant reindeer-carrier — until the younger brother is torn asunder by the great serdlernak bird whose pouch is full of seal-bones. The sister kills it with her boot, singles out the bones, and carries them home moving in her hand until the brother revives, seemingly quite unhurt.
summary.zh: 嬰兒一落地便露出巨齒，咬傷接生婆的手臂；怪物拖著披頭散髮的生母，吃盡全村——啃斷船柱使避難者跌落，又令避難巨巖翻覆。兩兄弟與妹妹逃入糧倉，連夜逃過謀害他們的屋舍，以兄長的靴子加咒封死一戶之門；最後借宿半鹿在肩的巨人——幼弟卻被捕豹的巨鳥賽德勒納克撕裂。妹妹以靴擊殺巨鳥，從其滿貯豹骨的嗉囊中揀出兄弟的骨頭，攜行途中骨已蠕動——一到家，兄弟便復原如初。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: such monsters generally figure as revengers of atrocity — in one version the imbecile child Tungavik devours all its housemates except two orphans who showed kindness. Graphic devouring recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Amongst a number of people who lived in the same house, one woman was in the act of childbirth when all of a sudden the midwife attending her cried out in great dismay, 'Ah, it is a monster, with great big teeth; it is tearing my arm!' As she spoke, all the inmates fled away to the boat, which was turned keel upwards, and to the top of a great rock; only two boys with their sister could find no room there, and they therefore hurried out to the provision-house. Meantime the monster appeared, dragging along his own mother, her hair all loose and flying about her, and it soon turned upon those on the boat: not being able itself to climb, it ate away the pillars beneath, so that, when they gave way, all the people came tumbling down and were devoured. It next came to the rock, and those who had taken refuge on it pushed and knocked against each other for horror, till all but one lost their footing and came down heads over heels; the monster now ordered the rock to upset, and the very last of them was made away with.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When these were all killed, the beast turned against the provision-house, but stopping, entered the main house instead; this process was repeated several times, and it always remained inside a little longer each time. During the last interval the children fled out of sight, and went far into the country until they came in sight of a house; they went in and told their story and the cause of their flight, and stayed there for the night. Most of the inmates had gone to sleep; the sister, however, did not dare to do so, and kept awake. At midnight she heard some one saying, 'They have probably themselves put their housemates to death, though they tell us a different story. The safest thing will be to have them killed in the morning.' At this speech she got greatly alarmed, and when the others had gone off to sleep she roused her brothers, and once more they fled on and reached another house, where they met the very same fate. But when they made their escape from this place the second night, the sister took one of her brother's boots and thrust it several times against the house-door, at the same time pronouncing a spell, that the people within might all perish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pursuing their way, they fell in with a man of extraordinary size, carrying one half of a reindeer on his shoulders; the sister said to the youngest brother, 'Go and try to make him understand why we have come here,' telling him how to put his words. When the boy had finished, the big man took them along to his own house, the interior nicely furnished and hung with reindeer-skins all along the walls; there they remained and made a meal upon some dry meat. This done, the girl said to her brothers, 'Reindeer-meat is good eating, no doubt; but what would make it eat still better?' — 'Mixing it up with some nice partridges, to be sure' — off they went, a flapping of wings presently heard, and lots of birds brought into the house. 'Partridges are very nice, sure enough; but what would make them eat still better?' — 'Mixing them up with some nice hares, to be sure!' — and so they went on with all kinds of game and fowls, until at last she said, 'Young serdlernaks are exceedingly nice, but the large ones — oh, be quick, be quick!' The huge man said, 'I never hunted that fowl without some misgivings; when she is hatching her eggs on the lee side of yonder point, and catches the seals, she is rather dangerous.' Still they all ran out to have a look at it; but seeing it perched on its rock, and sometimes rising to snatch at them, they were afraid and again retired — only the younger brother remained, and was torn asunder by it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the sister shouted, 'It is now time for me to interfere,' upon which they all ran out together; she quickly pulled out her boot, struck at the bird with it, and killed it on the spot. She now cut it up, and found its pouch filled with seal-bones, among which she likewise found those of her brother; when these had all been singled out, she carried them with her. While she was yet on the way she felt them move; and when they got close to the house she put them down, and the brother quickly revived, seemingly quite unhurt, and they all of them reached home safely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Kivigtok: The Brother Who Would Not Come Home
title.zh: 奇維托克：不願歸家的兄長

region.en: Rock cave in an out-of-the-way place

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; an old manuscript, sample of a very popular subject, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A man's second son turns kivigtok — flees the society of mankind — and the family spends two summers searching until they find his reindeer-skin-lined rock cave, dragging home a whole deer. Given his word that he will follow on the last load down, he vanishes instead with the remaining provisions, and later terrifies the searchers by yelling from the summit of a steep and altogether inaccessible rock, how he got there they could not make out, and finding it impossible to follow him they were obliged to give him up for lost.
summary.zh: 某家的次子成了奇維托克——拋開人世遁入荒野。全家兩度放棄狩獵之夏四處尋找，終於發現他鋪著馴鹿皮的巖穴，穴中儲滿乾肉與皮張；他扛著整鹿而歸，立誓最後一趟搬運時隨家人下山——卻帶著剩下的存糧憑空消失。此後他立於絕不可攀的崖頂對尋找他的家人長嚎示威；他如何上去無人知曉，家人只得放棄，任他失踪。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok lore (supernatural swiftness, longevity, clairvoyance) recurs across the collection; this is a sample record per Rink.

passages.text: There was once a man who had several sons; of these, the second son turned kivigtok — that is, fled the society of mankind. This happened in the winter-time; but next summer the father, as well as his other sons, went away from home in order to search for the fugitive. In this manner summer went by and winter came round, but still they had not found him. When summer was again approaching, they made all preparations for another search, this time to other places, along another firth; late in autumn they at length chanced to find out his solitary abode, in an out-of-the-way place, after having traversed the country in every direction for ever so long. His habitation was a cave or hollow in a rock, the inside being covered with reindeer-skin, and the entrance carefully closed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the time of their arrival the kivigtok was still out hunting; but a little later they saw him advance towards the place from the inland, dragging a whole deer along with him. The brothers were lying in ambush for him; when he came close to them they seized hold of him, and he recognised them at once, giving a loud cry like that of a reindeer, and saying, 'Do let me off; I shan't flee.' The father now asked him to return with them, adding, 'This is the second summer in which we have given up our hunt in order to find thee out, and, now we have succeeded, thou really must come home with us' — 'Yes, that I will.' They remained in the cave during the night, enjoying each other's company; next day they had much to do with the things that had to be taken back, the store-room, besides his dwelling-place, being filled with dry meat and skins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Tying up bundles to be taken down one by one to the tent of his relatives, pitched at some distance near the firth by which they were to travel home, they wanted him to follow them with the first loads; he excused himself — 'When ye go down the last time I shall follow; but I must stay and take care of these things.' They went without him; but on their return the kivigtok had disappeared, and taken the remainder of the provisions with him, and the brothers grew exceedingly vexed with themselves that they had thus relied on his word, without leaving any one in charge of him — all too late.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time afterwards, when they had gone out again to look for him, he terrified them by yelling and howling at them from the summit of a steep and altogether inaccessible rock. How he had got there they could not make out, but finding it impossible to follow him, they were obliged to give him up for lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

title.en: Nagguanguak: The Wife in the Gull's Mound
title.zh: 納瓜恩瓜克：鷗丘中的妻子

region.en: Gull's mound and the ingnersuit house under ground
region.zh: 鷗丘與地下的因格內爾舒特人居所

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Left behind on purpose by scolding hunting companions, Nagguanguak is courted by a man stepping out of a gull's mound whose hill-house is walled with reindeer-skins, and bears him a son to be named Imitlungnarsunguak — 'It did not matter; he would take care to make a great huntsman of him.' Claiming the boy's first catch, the father pulls the first seal through the floor of the passage; the mother shouts her son's garments out of the house and follows them down beneath the lifted coast-ice to the ingnersuit house under ground, where she finds him tied hands and feet, loosens him, hurries him into his clothes, and brings him away.
summary.zh: 被斥責她的獵伴故意丟下的納瓜恩瓜克，被一名自鷗丘中現身的男子娶為妻；丘中之屋四壁掛滿馴鹿皮，舒適異常。她為他生子，父親要為孩子取名伊米特隆納孫瓜克——『無妨，我會把他調教成偉大的獵手』，並索要孩子的頭獵。第一頭海豹竟從甬道地板下被拽走；母親高喊讓兒子的衣物自己飛出屋外，追著它們下到升起的海冰之下——地底的因格內爾舒特人屋中，她尋見被縛手縛腳的兒子，解開繩索、披上衣物，帶他逃了出來。

sensitivity.note: Ingnersuit (ingnersuat): elves or spirits having their abodes in the rocks along the sea (Rink's note). Parallel to the atliarusek corpus (cross-ref inuit-girl-atliarusek-husband).

passages.text: It once happened that two men went out deer-hunting, accompanied by a woman. On the way they scolded her, at which she got vexed, and tied up her boots in order to remain behind; they waited a while for her, but at length went along without her, and soon lost sight of her, as she had purposely hidden herself behind some large heaps of stones. She heard them seeking for her close beside her hiding-place, and lamenting their loss; but nevertheless she remained quiet until they were gone. When she was thus left alone she crept forth and went off in an opposite direction. After some time she came to a gull's mound, and observed a man coming out from it; she tried to escape, but he seized hold of her, and asked her to follow him to his dwelling-place in the gull's-hill, as he wished to marry her. She followed him reluctantly; but when he opened it to her, she noticed that it was covered with reindeer-skins on the walls, and on the whole looked quite comfortable. She now left off crying, entered the hill, and became his wife, and in due time she bore him a child, whom the father wanted to be named Imitlungnarsunguak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The wife remonstrated, saying that she had not got any relatives of that name; but the husband answered her, 'It did not matter; he would take care to make a great huntsman of him' — and then she let him call the boy as he liked. When he grew on, and his mother had spent a good many winters in this place, she longed for her former home and wished to return; the husband merely answered her, 'I claim his first catch, mind!' and then she left him along with her son, and went back to her old relatives and housemates, and once more lived with them. When the other children played with her son, she used to tell them not to do him any harm, and for fear of his unknown father they desisted. When he was quite grown up and saw the men prepare for the hunt, he was very desirous to join them; his mother observing this went outside and shouted out aloud, 'Now get him some tools!' — when she came out next morning she found them lying on the ground close beside the entry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the son brought home what he had caught for the first time, she again went out and cried with all her might, 'Imitlungnarsunguak has caught a seal!' — and when she was about to re-enter, the people were all very busy in dragging this seal into the house; when they had reached the farther end of the passage it could not be lifted across the threshold into the room, but rolled back, and in no time had vanished — the father, of course, had taken it away. His next catch the mother got; but when he went out hunting the third time, he remained away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother now mended his clothes and put them to rights, and in the evening went outside as before, shouting something at the pitch of her voice, upon which his garments came flying out of the house, and she hurried after them; when they had got as far as the beach, the coast-ice appeared to be lifted up, and left room for the clothes to slip down beneath — the mother following them closely. She now came to a house under ground belonging to ingnersuit, and there found her son, tied hands and feet; loosening him she hurried him into his clothes, and brought him away with her. Her own name was Nagguanguak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Children of Two Cousins: The Pet Calf and the Jealous Bow
title.zh: 兩表兄弟的孩子：寵鹿與嫉妒之弓

region.en: Shared winter-station and the strong man's coast
region.zh: 共用的越冬地與大力士的海岸

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two childless cousins part with 'we will see who first gets a child.' One prospers south and fathers a boy; the other, childless still, trains a young deer until it understands human speech. When the calf knocks the playmate-boy over once too often, the boy's father shoots it — dearly as he loves his cousin — and the childless man, furious, meets him armed with bows and shoots him on the spot, then drowns himself in tears. The orphan son returns full-grown, too late for the murderer, and kills instead the enormously strong wife-robber, restoring the women to their husbands.
summary.zh: 一對膝下無子的表兄弟分別時約定：『且看誰先得子。』南行的表弟得子；留守的表兄依舊無嗣，馴養一頭幼鹿直至通曉人言。小鹿與小主人嬉戲，卻屢屢把他撞翻——孩子的父親雖深愛表兄，仍舉弓射殺幼鹿；暴怒的無子者立即應戰，弓箭相見，當場射殺表弟，隨後痛哭失聲。遺孤長成後返鄉復仇，仇人已亡；轉而挑戰搶妻的巨力者，將其摔殺，把被搶的婦女一一送還其夫。

sensitivity.note: Killing and grief recorded as told in the 1875 source. The trained-calf motif parallels the animal-training sledge tales.

passages.text: There were once two cousins living together at the same winter-station, and at the time their wives were both childless. In spring they parted from each other, saying, 'Well, we will see who first gets a child.' One travelled away to the south, and established himself for the coming winter; at this place he lived in prosperity, and his wife bore him a child. When the boy grew up, the father took a fancy to return to his cousin; he, however, had still no children, and for this reason he caught a young deer and trained it up for his amusement — at length it improved so much that it could understand human speech. About that period the cousin returned, and first beheld the calf running about outside the house; the cousins once more lived together, and the boy and the calf became playmates. The calf, however, soon grew stronger, and sometimes knocked over the boy, at which he wept; for this reason the boy's father went and shot the calf, though he loved his cousin dearly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The childless man got into a great rage at this, and at once challenged his cousin, and they met armed with their bows; the childless man shot his cousin on the spot, but was very much afflicted afterwards, and burst into a flood of tears. The son of the man that had been thus killed removed to a distance, for he could not endure the sight of his father's cousin. When he was full-grown and strong he returned to the place, but he had come too late — the cousin was no more. He heard some rumour of an enormously strong man who used to rob other men of their wives; he challenged him to a wrestling-match, and overcame and killed him, and returned the women to their own husbands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl Who Was Stolen by an Inorusek
title.zh: 被內陸巨人擄走的少女

region.en: Salmon river highlands and the inorusek huts
region.zh: 鮭魚河高地與內陸巨人的營地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; obscure and fragmentary, related to tales 28 and 30, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried inland by an inorusek while salmon-fishing, a girl is fed deer-heart fat and tallow she will not touch, and warned by a bones-and-joints skeleton — once a stolen girl like her, whose boots were filled with reptiles until the flesh was all gone. The giant flings the crawling boots away into the corner, and at last she wins his trust — 'I have no intention of leaving thee now' — escapes over the hills to her parents' tent, bursting through the door-curtain: 'Let us be off at once and remove to some other place; the inlanders are sure to come and seek me here' — and the family never again ventured to pitch their tents on the continent.
summary.zh: 採鮭時被內陸巨人擄走的少女，拒食鹿心脂與普通油脂；一具瘦骨嶙峋的「人形」爬過長凳警告她：『別哭了，免得他們像對我那樣對你——當年他們把我的靴子裝滿蟲豸，脫下時，我的肉已經沒了。』巨人把蠕動的靴子擲向屋角，她才止住啼哭。她假意溫順——『我無意離開你』——趁其出獵翻山越嶺直奔父母帳篷，撞破門簾而入：『快搬走吧！內陸人一定會來找我的。』全家遷往外海小島，從此再不敢在大陸紮營。

sensitivity.note: Inorusek: fabulous giant-like inlanders (Rink's note). Details in the different manuscripts of tales 28, 30, and 43 are confounded and intermixed per Rink. The vermin-boots punishment recorded as told.

passages.text: A brother and a sister once lived together, and were very much attached to each other. The sister, very desirous of going off for the salmon-fishing, asked her brother to take her up to a salmon river; not being able to deny her, he put the boat into the sea and went with her to the fishing-place — but when they had landed and discharged the boat, putting all their things on the beach, she climbed a little way up the rocks and went across a smooth level to the brook. All at once she saw an inorusek close beside her; stupefied with terror, she tried to escape, but he caught hold of her and carried her further and further inland. The others plainly heard her shrieks for help, and hurried off to rescue her; but she was already gone, and her cries soon died away among the mountains. In the meantime the inorusek carried her up through the highlands till they stopped at a place with a number of huts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He intended to marry her, but first brought her to the house of a neighbour, where he put her down on the ledge and seated himself in front of her; she cried incessantly, but whenever she tried to run away he took hold of her like a little child and put her down again. While she was thus sitting an old woman peeped across the screen of the ledge, asking her, 'What wouldst thou like to eat? Dost thou like talu?' — the unhappy girl thought to herself, 'I wonder what talu is like!' She soon heard the old woman step down to fetch something, and though still weeping, peeped through her fingers, and perceived it to be the fat of a deer's heart they were giving her; however, she would not take it, and the old woman again retired. 'Wouldst thou like some ernowt?' — 'What may it be like?' — this time she saw the old hag produce some common tallow, saying, 'Now do eat that and be quiet'; but she would not take that either. Being very disheartened she continued to weep; the old woman now menaced her and threatened to take away her boots, at which she cried still more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she heard a rattling noise, and peeping through her fingers saw a strange figure, all bones and joints, creeping along the ledge towards her. This creature warned her, saying, 'Leave off crying, lest they should treat thee as they did me. I was once like thee; I was stolen and brought to this place, and because I would not leave off crying, they took away my boots and gave me others filled with reptiles, spiders, and vermin. They fastened them on my legs, and when they were taken off, the flesh was all gone.' When the skeleton had done speaking, she cried all the more; the old hag now in an outburst of ill temper and vexation approached, and she saw her holding a pair of boots in which she observed something crawling about — but the giant took hold of them and flung them away into the corner of the room, and then at length she was able to leave off crying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Her husband, however, kept a close watch upon her, and led her by the hand whenever she wished to go out. One day she said to him, 'Don't go on watching me so; I have no intention of leaving thee now; I like thee very much, and thou mayst safely leave me and go out deer-hunting as usual.' After that she feigned to go behind the house, but started from her hiding-place and ran up and down hill, and continued running towards the coast until she reached the tent of her parents, where she burst right through the door-curtain, not giving herself time to draw it before entering. She hastened to say, 'Let us be off at once and remove to some other place; the inlanders are sure to come and seek me here.' They at once left the mainland to settle down on one of the farthest-off islets; and after that time they never again ventured to pitch their tents on the continent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.
